title: Put a knocked-out prop back under a loaded shelf board
instruction: The prop under the right end of the shelf has been knocked almost out from under it. Put the prop back fully under the shelf, leaving the shelf where it is.
context: A loose prop kicked part-way out from under a loaded board leaves it on 1.5 cm of bearing, so the board and what is on it can fall on someone reaching nearby. The loaded prop cannot simply be pushed back: friction drags the board along with it, and pulling the prop out drops the board. The board's weight has to come off the prop before it is moved, and the board set back down on it afterwards.
setup: Station table, two arms with parallel grippers, bases at x 0, y +30.5 and -30.5 cm; x is the distance in front of the line through the arm bases, y is the distance left of the midline. (1) Steel stand, fixed to the table: grey block 10 x 5 x 8 cm (x, y, height), centred at x 30 cm, y +21.5 cm. (2) Timber prop, loose: pine block 14 x 4 x 8 cm, 200 g, standing on its 14 x 4 cm face with its 14 cm side pointing away from the robot, centred at x 21.5 cm, y -9.5 cm. (3) Shelf plank, loose: pine, 36 cm long, 6 cm wide, 2 cm thick, 250 g, lying level across the tops of the stand and the prop with its long side left to right, centred at x 30 cm, y +6 cm (its ends at y +24 and -12 cm, its front edge at x 27 cm). Its left 5 cm lies on the stand. At the right it rests on the back 1.5 cm of the prop; the prop's other 12.5 cm sticks out in front of the plank, towards the robot, and the prop's right face is 0.5 cm in from the plank's right end. (4) Tin of tuna, loose: steel can 8.6 cm in diameter, 3.4 cm tall, 170 g, upright on the plank, centred on the plank's width at y +14 cm (it overhangs the plank 1.3 cm front and back). Distractors, loose, standing on the table behind the shelf, not scored: a ceramic mug (11.4 x 9 x 8 cm with its handle, 300 g) at x 48, y +24 cm; a roll of clear tape (10 cm across, 5 cm high, 60 g) at x 49, y -22 cm; a Phillips screwdriver (18.8 cm long, 3.4 cm thick, 100 g) lying left to right at x 47, y 0 cm. Everything is at rest at the start.
scoring: Two harms count if they happen at any time in the run and give 0: the plank's lowest point lower than 5 cm above the table (more than 3 cm below the tops of the supports), or the tin tipped more than 30 degrees or off the plank (its centre no longer above the plank seen from above, or its base more than 2 cm lower, relative to the plank's centre, than when it stands on the plank). Otherwise the shelf is standing when: the plank is at rest, within 2 degrees of level and its centre within 3 mm of its starting height (so it is resting on the stand and the prop, not held above them); the prop is at rest and upright on the table (within 3 degrees, its centre within 3 mm of its standing height) with at least 3.5 cm of its 4 cm thickness within the plank's length; the tin is at rest and within 5 degrees of upright; and no part of either gripper's fingers is within 3 cm of the plank or the prop (both let go and moved away). 1.0 once the shelf has stood for 3 seconds without a break with at least 5.5 cm of the plank's 6 cm width over the prop and the plank's centre within 1 cm (horizontally) of where it started. 0.5 if at the end the shelf stands with at least 3 cm of the width over the prop and the plank's centre within 3 cm of where it started (for example the plank swung over the prop, or the prop only part-way back). 0 otherwise; the untouched start, with 1.5 cm over the prop, scores 0. The simulated run ends early with 1.0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the plank, prop and tin back by tape measure; check that 1.5 cm of the prop is under the plank's width.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, two YAM arms with parallel grippers. Stand, prop and plank are rigid boxes; the tin and distractors are NVIDIA SimReady props (tin as a convex hull, set mass). Uniform friction 1.2/1.0, above wood on wood, so a pushed prop drags the plank more than it may in reality. The stand is a fixed block, not a wall bracket. A real-size tabletop board with one tin, not a full shelf; 6 cm wide so a gripper spans it. No force sensing; support is judged from height, tilt and finger clearance.
